title: Present perfect continuous and present perfect

sections.title: Activity in progress until recently/now
sections.content:
We use the present perfect continuous to express the idea of an activity in progress until recently or until the time of speaking. It may continue beyond this point:
• Have you been working in the garden all day? You look exhausted.
• She's been writing the book since she was in her twenties and at last it's finished.
Note that we often use time expressions to say how long the activity has been in progress.
We don't use the present perfect continuous with verbs such as belong, know, (dis)like, and understand that describe unchanging states:
• Have you known each other long? (not Have you been knowing ...)
• I haven't liked ice cream since I ate too much and was sick. (not I haven't been liking ...)
When we talk about situations (general characteristics or circumstances) existing up to the present we can often use either the present perfect or present perfect continuous:
• We've been looking forward to this holiday for ages. (or We've looked forward to ...)

sections.title: Extended activity vs rapid completion
sections.content:
We often use the present perfect or the present perfect continuous to talk about something that has recently finished if we can still see its results. However, we generally use the present perfect continuous with verbs that suggest extended or repeated activity. Compare:
• He's broken his finger and is in a lot of pain. (not He's been breaking ...) and
• I've been playing squash and need a shower! (more likely than I've played ...)
We use the present perfect continuous rather than the present perfect when we draw a conclusion from what we can see, hear, etc. We often use this form to complain or criticise:
• Who's been messing around with my papers? They're all over the place.
• You've been eating chocolate, haven't you? There's some on your shirt.
When we talk about the result of circumstances or an activity, we use the present perfect, rather than the present perfect continuous. When we focus on the process we often use either the present perfect or the present perfect continuous. Compare:
• Prices have decreased by 7%. (not Prices have been decreasing by 7%.) and
• Prices have been decreasing recently. (or Prices have decreased ...)
• I've used three tins of paint on the kitchen walls. (not I've been using three tins of paint on the kitchen walls.) and
• I've been using a new kind of paint on the kitchen walls. (or I've used ...)

sections.title: Ongoing/repeated vs completed/specified
sections.content:
The present perfect continuous emphasises that an activity is ongoing and repeated, while the present perfect suggests the activity happened only once or on a specified number of occasions:
• Miguel has been kicking a football against the wall all day. (more likely than ... has kicked ...)
• He has played for the national team in 65 matches so far. (not He has been playing for the national team in 65 matches so far.)
Compare:
• The workers have been calling for the chairman's resignation. (= emphasises a number of times, probably over an extended period) and
• Workers have called for management to begin negotiations on pay. (= maybe a number of times or only once.)

exercises.question: Martina Gonzalez ___ in a rented flat since returning to Buenos Aires.
exercises.hint: Focus on the ongoing process/extended activity over a period.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: has been staying
We use the present perfect continuous here to emphasise an ongoing or recently continuing activity.
💡 Focus on the ongoing process/extended activity over a period.

exercises.question: We ___ at this hotel a couple of times before.
exercises.hint: A specified number of occasions ('a couple of times').
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have stayed
A specified number of occasions ('a couple of times'). The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: All day, the police ___ motorists to question them about the accident.
exercises.hint: Ongoing and repeated activity ('All day').
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have been stopping
We use the present perfect continuous here to emphasise an ongoing or recently continuing activity.
💡 Ongoing and repeated activity ('All day').

exercises.question: Good, the noise ___. I can start concentrating on my work again.
exercises.hint: Completed single event with a present result.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: has stopped
Completed single event with a present result. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: I'm exhausted. I ___ (work) all day without a break.
exercises.hint: Emphasis on duration of continuous activity up to now → present perfect continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have been working
The present perfect continuous emphasises the duration of an ongoing activity. 'All day' is the key duration signal. The tiredness is the present result of the extended activity.

exercises.question: I ___ any of Dickens' novels. (read - negative)
exercises.hint: Talking about general life experience or result.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: haven't read
Talking about general life experience or result.

exercises.question: I ___ this book on astrophysics for hours and I'm still only on page six.
exercises.hint: Focus on the process ('for hours') and it's incomplete.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have been reading
We use the present perfect continuous here to emphasise an ongoing or recently continuing activity.
💡 Focus on the process ('for hours') and it's incomplete.

exercises.question: Dr Fletcher ___ the same lecture to students for the last ten years. (give)
exercises.hint: Ongoing repeated action over an extended period.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: has been giving
We use the present perfect continuous here to emphasise an ongoing or recently continuing activity.
💡 Ongoing repeated action over an extended period.

exercises.question: Mr Sato ___ nearly a million pounds to the charity this year.
exercises.hint: Focus on the result (quantity: nearly a million pounds).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: has given
Focus on the result (quantity: nearly a million pounds). The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: Someone ___ (eat) my sandwich! Half of it is gone.
exercises.hint: Completed action with present evidence (half gone) → present perfect simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: has eaten
Use the present perfect simple when the action is complete and the focus is on the present result or evidence. The sandwich being half-gone is the visible consequence.

exercises.question: I did 20 lengths of the pool today. I ___ that far since I was at school. (swim - negative)
exercises.hint: State of not having done the activity, general experience.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: haven't swum
State of not having done the activity, general experience.

exercises.question: I ___ and I feel exhausted.
exercises.hint: Recently finished extended activity causing a present result/conclusion.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have been swimming
We use the present perfect continuous here to emphasise an ongoing or recently continuing activity.
💡 Recently finished extended activity causing a present result/conclusion.

exercises.question: In recent years, companies ___ increasing resources into internet marketing.
exercises.hint: General circumstance/trend existing up to the present.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have been putting
We use the present perfect continuous here to emphasise an ongoing or recently continuing activity.
💡 General circumstance/trend existing up to the present.

exercises.question: The South African coal company ___ the Calverton Mine up for sale.
exercises.hint: Single completed event.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: has put
Single completed event. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: How long ___ (you / study) English?
exercises.hint: Question about duration of ongoing activity → present perfect continuous preferred.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have you been studying
With 'how long' and an activity that is still ongoing, the present perfect continuous is preferred because it emphasises the continuous duration up to now.

exercises.question: An important file ___ from my office.
exercises.hint: Single completed event.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: has disappeared
Single completed event. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: Plants and vegetables ___ from my garden since we had new neighbours.
exercises.hint: Repeated, ongoing occurrences.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have been disappearing
We use the present perfect continuous here to emphasise an ongoing or recently continuing activity.
💡 Repeated, ongoing occurrences.

exercises.question: '...and in 1957 alone around 6,000 people have been dying.' Correct?
exercises.hint: A completed number ('6,000 people') in a finished past period ('1957 alone').
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Should be 'died' (past simple) or 'have died'
A completed number ('6,000 people') in a finished past period ('1957 alone'). The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: '...producing over a hundred books...' - 'we have been producing over a hundred books'. Correct?
exercises.hint: When we focus on the result/number produced ('over a hundred books'), use present perfect.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Should be 'have produced'
When we focus on the result/number produced ('over a hundred books'), use present perfect. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: She ___ (write) three novels. Her latest is brilliant.
exercises.hint: Completed, countable achievements → present perfect simple (not continuous).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: has written
When talking about completed, countable achievements ('three novels'), use the present perfect simple. The continuous would suggest the writing is still ongoing.

exercises.question: '...in 2012 they have been awarding the National Prize...' Correct?
exercises.hint: A specific single finished event in a finished past time ('in 2012').
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Should be 'awarded' (past simple)
A specific single finished event in a finished past time ('in 2012').

exercises.question: 'It is a tragedy that the government has been making this decision now.' Correct?
exercises.hint: A single completed decision, not an ongoing process.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Should be 'has made'
A single completed decision, not an ongoing process. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: '...the present government has been announcing this cut...' Correct?
exercises.hint: A single completed action.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Should be 'has announced'
A single completed action. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: '...I have been finding evidence that they...' Correct?
exercises.hint: Focus on the completed result of the search ('finding evidence').
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Should be 'have found'
Focus on the completed result of the search ('finding evidence').

exercises.question: 'I have been speaking to the Minister about this yesterday...' Correct?
exercises.hint: A finished action in a finished past time frame ('yesterday').
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Should be 'spoke'
A finished action in a finished past time frame ('yesterday').

exercises.question: '...and have also been writing to the Prime Minister demanding...' Correct?
options: Should be 'have also written' or 'also wrote'
Should be 'have also written' or 'also wrote'ing
exercises.hint: Likely a single completed letter.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Should be 'have also written' or 'also wrote'
Likely a single completed letter.
